projects.title: Signal lamp

brief.goal: Program the robot's LED and buzzer to send a message that a stranger could read without you explaining it — an SOS, a countdown to launch, or a mood that changes.
brief.metric: Someone watching the sim can name what the pattern is trying to say, and you can point to the part of the program that makes each beat.
constraints: Sim only — no hardware yet
Use only the LED, buzzer, and wait blocks you have met
The pattern must repeat cleanly, not run once and stop
evidence: The sim run captured (screen recording or screenshot)
The program exported from the editor
One or two sentences saying what the pattern communicates

rubric.label: The pattern runs in the simulator
You explained what it communicates

projects.simMilestone: LED pattern verified in the simulator

projects.title: Polygon plotter

brief.goal: Write one program that draws a triangle, a square, a hexagon, and an octagon — and switches between them by changing a single number, not by rewriting the code.
brief.metric: Setting the number of sides to 3, 4, 6, and 8 produces a clean closed shape each time, with no leftover gap or overlap.
constraints: Sim only, pen down
Exactly one number changes between shapes — everything else stays put
Use a loop; do not unroll the sides by hand
evidence: A table mapping each side count to the shape and turn angle it produced
A short explanation of the 360 ÷ n relationship in your own words
The four sim drawings

rubric.label: All four shapes draw from one changed number
You explained why the turn is 360 ÷ n

projects.simMilestone: Four shapes drawn from one parameter in the simulator

projects.title: Don't crash

brief.goal: Write one program that keeps the robot moving without hitting anything, and make it good enough that it survives arenas you have never seen — not just the one you practised on.
brief.metric: Runs for 60 simulated seconds with no collision in at least 4 of 5 randomised arenas.
constraints: Sim only, graded across 5 seeded worlds
A fixed move-turn sequence will fail — you must react to the distance sensor
Choose one threshold and use it deliberately
evidence: The pass/fail result for each of the 5 seeds
A written justification of why your threshold is the number it is, not something bigger or smaller
A note on which seed was hardest and why

rubric.label: Survives at least 4 of 5 seeded arenas
You justified your chosen threshold

projects.simMilestone: Survives at least 4 of 5 seeded arenas for 60 seconds

projects.title: Strong or fast

brief.goal: On the real chassis, find out what you trade away for speed: time a 1 m run at three speed settings and see how steep a slope the robot can still climb.
brief.metric: You have a filled measurement table for all three speeds plus the incline test, and your written prediction is recorded before any measurement was taken.
constraints: Real hardware — Kit 1 chassis
Predict every result in writing before you measure it
Same 1 m course and same battery charge for all three speed runs
evidence: A photo of your measurement setup
A table of predicted vs actual time for each speed and the incline result
An explanation of where prediction and reality disagreed, and why

rubric.label: Photo of the real measurement setup
Completed measurement table
Prediction recorded first and the gap explained

projects.simMilestone: Drivetrain speed-vs-torque comparison verified in the simulator
projects.realMilestone: Time three 1 m runs at different speeds and one incline test on the real chassis.

projects.title: Two-mode robot

brief.goal: Build a robot with two clear modes: it patrols until it detects something, then chases it, then returns to patrolling when it loses it — built as an explicit state machine, not a tangle of ifs.
brief.metric: The robot switches modes correctly in the sim across seeded worlds and again on the real micro:bit chassis, and every mode change in the run matches an arrow on your diagram.
constraints: Real hardware — micro:bit robot
Structure must be an explicit state machine with named states
Each transition must have a condition you can point to
evidence: A hand-drawn or Mermaid state diagram of the modes and transitions
A video of the real robot patrolling, chasing, and recovering
A note confirming the diagram matches the built program

rubric.label: State diagram matches the built program
Video shows all three modes working

projects.simMilestone: State machine passes seeded worlds in the simulator
projects.realMilestone: Run the patrol-chase-recover state machine on the real micro:bit robot.

projects.title: Port it

brief.goal: Take your "Don't crash" program, rewrite it in text code, and get it running on the real robot so it dodges a real obstacle — then explain what reality did that the simulator never did.
brief.metric: The typed program passes the sim milestone and the real robot avoids a physical obstacle on video, with a written account of every sim-vs-real difference you noticed.
constraints: Real hardware; program written in text, not blocks
Behaviour must come from the same logic as P3, ported not redesigned
Test with a real obstacle, not a hand waved in front of it
evidence: A video of the real robot avoiding a real obstacle
A writeup comparing simulator behaviour to real behaviour and why they differ
The ported text program

rubric.label: Video shows the real robot avoiding an obstacle
You compared simulator and real behaviour

projects.simMilestone: P3 rewritten in text passes the sim grader
projects.realMilestone: Flash the ported text program and have the real robot avoid a physical obstacle.

projects.title: Race the line

brief.goal: Tune a line follower on the real robot until it is both accurate and fast — and keep a log of every change so the tuning itself becomes the thing you can prove you did.
brief.metric: Hits the target line-accuracy and the time target on the real course, backed by a tuning log showing the gains you tried and what each one changed.
constraints: Real hardware — real line course
Change one knob at a time and record the outcome before the next change
Both the accuracy target and the time target must be met, not one or the other
evidence: The tuning log: every gain tried, what happened, what you changed next
A video of a passing run
The final accuracy and time figures

rubric.label: Tuning log records every gain and outcome
Video shows a run meeting both targets

projects.simMilestone: Line accuracy reaches the target in the simulator
projects.realMilestone: Tune the line follower to hit both accuracy and time targets on the real course.

projects.title: Return to base

brief.goal: Send the real robot out on a route and bring it back to where it started, within a tolerance you set yourself — three times — then account for exactly where the leftover error came from.
brief.metric: All three out-and-back runs land within your stated tolerance of the start, and your error budget adds up to roughly the error you actually measured.
constraints: Real hardware; three separate runs
State your tolerance target and justify it before running
Measure the real end-position error each time — do not estimate it by eye
evidence: The measured end-position error for each of the three runs
An estimated error budget naming where each bit of drift came from
Your stated tolerance target and why you chose it

rubric.label: End-position error measured for each run
Error budget accounts for the drift

projects.simMilestone: Returns within tolerance across seeded worlds in the simulator
projects.realMilestone: Complete three measured out-and-back runs on the real robot within your stated tolerance.

projects.title: Maze solver

brief.goal: Write one program that can solve mazes it has never seen — ten unseen seeds — and does it with paths that are close to the shortest possible, not just paths that eventually work.
brief.metric: Solves at least 8 of 10 unseen maze seeds, scored on how close your path length is to the optimal path.
constraints: Graded on unseen seeds you cannot practise on
One program must handle all ten — no per-maze tweaks
Efficiency counts: a solution that wanders scores below one that plans
evidence: The solve/fail result for each of the 10 seeds
The path-efficiency ratio against the optimal path length
A photo or video if you built the tape maze on the floor (stretch)

rubric.label: Solves at least 8 of 10 unseen mazes
Path efficiency reported against optimal

projects.simMilestone: Solves at least 8 of 10 unseen maze seeds in the simulator
projects.realMilestone: Solve a tape maze on the floor with the real robot (stretch goal), captured on video.

projects.title: Follow the colour

brief.goal: Make the robot track a coloured target with its camera and keep it centred as it moves — then go hunting for the ways it breaks, because knowing when vision fails is half the skill.
brief.metric: Keeps the target inside the centre band above the tracking threshold in good conditions, and you have documented five distinct conditions that defeat it.
constraints: Real hardware — camera tracking
Working once in good light is not passing
Each failure in the catalogue must be a genuinely different cause
evidence: A video of the robot tracking the target
A failure catalogue of five conditions that break it, each with a photo
A note on which failures you could fix and which are fundamental

rubric.label: Video shows the target tracked and centred
Five photographed failure conditions catalogued

projects.simMilestone: Target tracked above the threshold in the simulator
projects.realMilestone: Track a coloured target with the real camera and keep it centred on video.

projects.title: Teach it something

brief.goal: Pick a 2-3 class problem the robot can sense, collect your own data, train a tiny classifier, and report how well it really does on data it was never trained on — honestly.
brief.metric: You report held-out accuracy with a confusion matrix from a proper train/test split; an honest low number scores higher here than an inflated high one.
constraints: Real hardware for data collection
Any result without a train/test split is an automatic revise-and-resubmit
Report accuracy on held-out data only, never on training data
evidence: A description of the dataset: classes, features, how many samples
A confusion matrix from the held-out test set
The honest test accuracy, with a note on what it gets wrong

rubric.label: Dataset, classes, and features described
Confusion matrix from held-out data
Honest held-out accuracy reported

projects.simMilestone: Classifier reaches the threshold on held-out data in the simulator
projects.realMilestone: Collect a labelled dataset from the real robot and train a classifier on it.

projects.title: Capstone

brief.goal: Choose your own robot to build. Write the brief yourself against the template — goal, success metric, constraints, test plan — get it accepted, then build it in sim, build it for real, and show it works.
brief.metric: Your brief is accepted against the rubric before you build, and the finished robot meets the success metric you set for it under your own test plan.
constraints: Your brief must be accepted before building starts
Deliver both a sim prototype and a real build
You are held to the standard you set, not one we set
evidence: A design document: goal, metric, constraints, test plan, results
A 2-minute demo video of the working build
A reflection on the whole year: what you learned and what you would do differently

rubric.label: Design doc with brief, test plan, and results
Two-minute demo video of the build
Year-end reflection written
